EC1.1.1.name: Door Accessibility
EC1.1.1.definition:
Doorways ≥ 90 cm; automated or manual operation ≤ 20 N; 
handle height 80–110 cm.
EC1.1.1.justification: Door accessibility is a fundamental physical access requirement. If doors are inaccessible, users may be unable to enter or move independently within the office building. It directly affects mobility, safety, evacuation, and daily usability.

EC1.1.2.name: Signage & Wayfinding for Mobility Users
EC1.1.2.definition: Clear directional signage at accessible height (max 160 cm); readable from wheelchair position.
EC1.1.2.justification: Signage is important for orientation and independent navigation, but it becomes meaningful only after physical access is achieved. In office environments, it supports usability rather than enabling basic entry.

EC1.2.1.name: Thermal Comfort Adaptability
EC1.2.1.definition: Temperature maintained between 20–24 °C; localized or user-controllable systems ensure comfort and safety.
EC1.2.1.justification: Thermal comfort strongly affects physical wellbeing, fatigue, circulation conditions, and overall usability for persons with mobility impairments who may remain indoors for extended periods.
levels: Smart Door Sensors & Assisted Opening Alerts
I-Powered Automatic Doors with Adaptive Force
Integrated Smart Accessibility Ecosystem (Digital Twin + Predictive Access)

EC1.2.2.name: Air Quality and Ventilation
EC1.2.2.definition: CO₂ < 1000 ppm, PM₂.₅ < 25 µg/m³; ventilation ensures consistent air renewal, monitored by smart sensors.
EC1.2.2.justification: Indoor air quality is critical in office buildings due to long occupancy periods. Poor IAQ directly affects health, concentration, respiratory comfort, and safety for vulnerable users.
levels: QR Code / NFC-Triggered Wayfinding (Low-Cost Digital Layer)
Smart Digital Signage with Adaptive Interfaces

EC1.2.3.name: Lighting and Glare Control
EC1.2.3.definition: Minimum 300 lux in circulation areas; glare index (UGR) < 19; adjustable illumination levels preferred.
EC1.2.3.justification: Proper lighting supports safe movement, spatial awareness, and reduced visual strain. Glare reduction is especially important in office environments with screens and circulation areas.

EC1.2.4.name: Smart Monitoring of Safety & Comfort
EC1.2.4.definition: Integrated digital systems or sensors continuously track IAQ, temperature, lighting, and noise, issuing alerts when thresholds are exceeded.
EC1.2.4.justification: Smart monitoring enhances operational control and preventive management, but it acts mainly as a supporting mechanism rather than a direct environmental condition itself.

EC1.3.1.name: Visual Connection to Key Points
EC1.3.1.definition: Major destinations (exits, lifts, restrooms) are visible or directly signposted from accessible routes.
EC1.3.1.justification: Direct visibility and clear signposting of major destinations are fundamental for efficient navigation and independent movement within office environments. This criterion has the greatest direct impact on orientation and usability.

EC1.3.2.name: Multisensory Navigation Support
EC1.3.2.definition: Wayfinding includes tactile maps, digital kiosks with voice output, or color-coded floor lines to aid orientation.
EC1.3.2.justification: Multisensory wayfinding systems significantly improve accessibility for users with cognitive, sensory, or mobility limitations by providing alternative navigation methods and reducing dependence on assistance.

EC1.3.3.name: Visibility and Lighting of Pathways
EC1.3.3.definition: Circulation zones maintain uniform lighting ≥ 300 lux, ensuring visibility of wayfinding cues and floor textures.
EC1.3.3.justification: Adequate lighting is essential for recognizing routes, textures, and signage; however, it primarily supports the effectiveness of the other navigation elements rather than functioning independently.
levels: Fixed Audio Beacons at Decision Points (Foundation Layer)

EC1.4.1.name: Low-Force Operation
EC1.4.1.definition: Buttons, touch surfaces, and doors require ≤ 20 N actuation force for ease of use by individuals with limited strength.
EC1.4.1.justification: Physical ease of operation is the most critical factor for users with limited strength, dexterity, or mobility impairments. If controls require excessive force, accessibility is fundamentally compromised.
levels: Predictive & Adaptive Visual Safety Ecosystem (Advanced Layer)

EC1.4.2.name: Haptic and Auditory Feedback
EC1.4.2.definition: Smart controls provide tactile or audio feedback to confirm successful operation without relying solely on vision.
EC1.4.2.justification: Multisensory feedback improves usability, confirmation of actions, and user confidence, especially when visual attention or motor precision is limited.

EC1.4.3.name: Control Response Time
EC1.4.3.definition: Device interfaces react within ≤ 1 s to inputs, avoiding double activation and frustration for slower motor users.
EC1.4.3.justification: Fast and reliable system response prevents repeated actions, frustration, and operational errors, supporting smoother interaction with smart building technologies.

EC1.5.1.name: Ergonomic Public Furniture
EC1.5.1.definition: Benches, desks, and tables provide 70 cm knee clearance and appropriate reach heights (80–110 cm).
EC1.5.1.justification: Ergonomically accessible furniture is fundamental for daily usability, comfort, and equal participation in office and shared public environments.

EC1.5.2.name: Rest and Interaction Points
EC1.5.2.definition: Resting zones every 30 m along outdoor or indoor public circulation routes with accessible seating.
EC1.5.2.justification: Accessible resting areas improve mobility endurance, reduce fatigue, and support social interaction, particularly in large office buildings and circulation areas.
levels: Predictive & Adaptive Calm Navigation System (Advanced Layer)

EC1.5.3.name: Adaptable Participation Equipment
EC1.5.3.definition: Tables, displays, and shared devices are height-adjustable and operable with one hand.
EC1.5.3.justification: Height-adjustable and one-hand operable equipment is critical for enabling active participation in meetings, collaborative workspaces, and shared services.

EC2.1.1.name: Hazard Warning Surfaces
EC2.1.1.definition: Tactile warning patterns (domes or ribs) before stairs, ramps, and intersections.
EC2.1.1.justification: Tactile warning surfaces are essential for safe movement and hazard detection, particularly near stairs, ramps, and circulation intersections. They provide continuous passive guidance throughout the building.

EC2.1.2.name: Auditory Guidance Systems
EC2.1.2.definition: Audio beacons or voice navigation at decision points and elevators.
EC2.1.2.justification: Audio guidance systems significantly improve independent navigation and orientation for visually impaired users, especially in complex office layouts and vertical circulation areas.

EC2.1.3.name: Visual Alerts for Alarms
EC2.1.3.definition: Alarm systems supported by synchronized flashing lights.
EC2.1.3.justification: Visual alarm systems are critical life-safety elements for users with hearing impairments, ensuring equal access to emergency notifications and evacuation information.
levels: Digital Twin for Accessibility Optimization (Advanced Layer)

EC2.2.1.name: Multisensory Alarm Systems
EC2.2.1.definition: Emergency alarms incorporate synchronized visual, audible, and vibration alerts to ensure inclusiveness for users with hearing or visual impairments.
EC2.2.1.justification: Multisensory alarms are the most critical criterion because they ensure emergency alerts are accessible to both hearing- and visually-impaired users, directly affecting life safety and inclusive evacuation.

EC2.2.2.name: Acoustic Signal Clarity
EC2.2.2.definition: Audible alarms and voice messages are intelligible with speech transmission index (STI) ≥ 0.6 and sound level ≥ 15 dB above ambient noise.
EC2.2.2.justification: Clear and intelligible audible communication is essential for emergency response, especially in office buildings with high background noise and complex circulation spaces.

EC2.2.3.name: Emergency Lighting for Low Vision
EC2.2.3.definition: Emergency lighting ensures minimum 1 lux along evacuation paths and uses warm-white tones to minimize glare.
EC2.2.3.justification: Proper emergency lighting supports safe evacuation, route visibility, and reduced disorientation for users with low vision during power failures or emergencies.

EC2.3.1.name: Multisensory Wayfinding System
EC2.3.1.definition: Circulation routes integrate tactile, auditory, and visual cues to guide users with different sensory needs.
EC2.3.1.justification: Continuous wayfinding support is fundamental for independent movement throughout the building during normal daily operation. It directly affects usability, orientation, and equal access to services and spaces.

EC2.3.2.name: Emergency Wayfinding Accessibility
EC2.3.2.definition: Escape routes and exit signage integrate tactile and audio features for multi-sensory evacuation support.
EC2.3.2.justification: Accessible emergency navigation is critical for safety and evacuation; however, it is activated mainly during emergency situations rather than throughout everyday building use.

EC2.4.1.name: Voice Command Functionality
EC2.4.1.definition: Core building functions (entry, lighting, elevators) include speech-recognition options for touch-free operation.
EC2.4.1.justification: Voice-enabled operation improves hands-free accessibility and usability for many users, particularly in smart office environments; however, it mainly supports operational convenience.

EC2.4.2.name: Captioning and Visual Alarms
EC2.4.2.definition: Audio messages and system alerts are accompanied by captions or visual indicators.
EC2.4.2.justification: Captioning and visual alerts are essential for ensuring equal access to information, notifications, and emergency communication for users with hearing impairments. This has the highest direct impact on safety and inclusiveness.

EC2.4.3.name: Personal Assistive Synchronization
EC2.4.3.definition: Smart systems connect with hearing aids, screen readers, or mobile accessibility apps for personalized usability.
EC2.4.3.justification: Integration with hearing aids, screen readers, and accessibility applications enhances personalized usability and supports independent interaction with building systems.

EC2.5.1.name: Hearing Loop and Assistive Systems
EC2.5.1.definition: Meeting rooms and auditoria are equipped with induction loops or compatible assistive hearing technologies.
EC2.5.1.justification: Assistive hearing systems are essential for equal participation in meetings, presentations, and collaborative office activities, directly affecting communication accessibility and inclusion.

EC2.5.2.name: High-Contrast Environmental Design
EC2.5.2.definition: Color contrast between walls, floors, and furniture ≥ 70% to enhance visual perception.
EC2.5.2.justification: High visual contrast significantly improves spatial recognition, orientation, and safety for users with low vision, especially in everyday circulation and workspace interaction.

EC2.5.3.name: Smart Sensory Adaptation
EC2.5.3.definition: Automated systems adjust lighting, volume, or visual cues based on ambient noise and brightness conditions.
EC2.5.3.justification: Adaptive smart systems enhance comfort and usability by dynamically adjusting environmental conditions; however, they mainly function as supportive optimization technologies.

EC3.1.1.name: Soothing Lighting & Color Temperature
EC3.1.1.definition: Avoids flicker and blue-rich lighting; color temperature 2700–4000 K.
EC3.1.1.justification: Lighting quality has a continuous and direct impact on sensory comfort, stress reduction, concentration, and wellbeing for neurodiverse users. Poor lighting conditions can significantly affect usability and comfort throughout the workday.

EC3.1.2.name: Navigational Cues Reinforced Digitally
EC3.1.2.definition: Indoor maps or apps include simplified “calm” mode with minimal distractions.
EC3.1.2.justification: Simplified digital navigation tools improve orientation and reduce cognitive overload, particularly in large or complex office environments; however, they act mainly as supportive navigation aids.

EC3.2.1.name: Predictable Environmental Transitions
EC3.2.1.definition: Gradual changes in lighting, sound, and temperature between zones prevent sensory overstimulation or confusion.
EC3.2.1.justification: Gradual environmental transitions are highly important for minimizing confusion, anxiety, and sensory overload when moving between office zones and circulation areas.

EC3.2.2.name: Acoustic and Visual Balance
EC3.2.2.definition: Environments maintain moderate sound levels (< 45 dB(A)) and neutral lighting to support focus and emotional regulation.
EC3.2.2.justification: Stable acoustic and visual conditions directly affect concentration, emotional regulation, stress reduction, and daily workplace comfort, making this the most influential criterion during routine occupancy.

EC3.2.3.name: Calm Emergency Waiting Areas
EC3.2.3.definition: Refuge and waiting areas are acoustically buffered and visually simple to prevent sensory distress during emergencies.
EC3.2.3.justification: Sensory-sensitive refuge areas are essential during emergencies, but their use is situational rather than continuous throughout everyday building operation.

EC3.3.1.name: Simplified Wayfinding Maps
EC3.3.1.definition: Floor maps use minimalistic graphic language and recognizable icons, avoiding information overload.
EC3.3.1.justification: Clear and simplified maps directly reduce cognitive overload, improve orientation, and support independent navigation for neurodiverse users in complex office environments.

EC3.3.2.name: Spatial Familiarity Across Floors
EC3.3.2.definition: Identical layout logic and wayfinding color codes are used on each floor for intuitive cross-level navigation.
EC3.3.2.justification: Consistent spatial organization and repeated wayfinding logic across floors significantly improve predictability, memory retention, and intuitive navigation, making this the most influential criterion for continuous building usability.

EC3.4.1.name: Visual Focus Stability
EC3.4.1.definition: Screen transitions avoid flashing or rapid animations; frame rates ≥ 60 Hz to prevent sensory overload.
EC3.4.1.justification: Stable visual interfaces are critical for preventing sensory overstimulation, distraction, fatigue, and discomfort. This criterion directly affects the daily usability of digital systems and smart interfaces.

EC3.4.2.name: Personalized User Profiles
EC3.4.2.definition: Smart systems allow saving of preferred settings for brightness, sound, and layout simplicity.
EC3.4.2.justification: Personalized settings enhance comfort and usability by adapting systems to individual sensory and cognitive preferences, but they function mainly as supportive customization features.

EC3.5.1.name: Low-Stimulus Participation Zones
EC3.5.1.definition: Dedicated quiet or low-sensory areas are available near shared spaces to support comfort and focus.
EC3.5.1.justification: Quiet and low-sensory spaces provide direct support for stress reduction, emotional regulation, concentration, and social participation, making them highly important in office environments.

EC3.5.2.name: Inclusive Color and Lighting Strategy
EC3.5.2.definition: Calming, non-flickering light sources (3000–4000 K) and neutral color schemes reduce cognitive load.
EC3.5.2.justification: Appropriate lighting and calming color schemes significantly reduce cognitive fatigue and sensory overload, while supporting comfort and focus throughout the workplace.

EC4.1.1.name: Color Temperature Regulation
EC4.1.1.definition: Warm light (<4000K) used in circulation and waiting zones to reduce stress.
EC4.1.1.justification: Warm and calming lighting conditions help reduce stress, anxiety, and emotional discomfort, supporting a more comfortable and psychologically supportive workplace environment.

EC4.1.2.name: Non-Verbal Wayfinding Aids
EC4.1.2.definition: Symbols, lighting cues, and visual beacons guide movement without text reliance.
EC4.1.2.justification: Non-verbal navigation cues significantly improve independent orientation and reduce confusion for users who may experience communication difficulties, cognitive stress, or language-processing challenges.

EC4.2.1.name: Stress-Reducing Lighting Design
EC4.2.1.definition: Lighting systems avoid flicker, provide warm color tones (2700–3500 K), and support calm visual environments.
EC4.2.1.justification: Lighting conditions continuously affect mood, stress levels, emotional comfort, and concentration throughout the working environment, making this the most influential criterion.

EC4.2.2.name: Smart Support Interfaces
EC4.2.2.definition: Digital systems provide empathetic tone, calm colors, and clear progress feedback to reduce frustration during interactions.
EC4.2.2.justification: Calm and supportive digital interaction systems significantly reduce frustration and cognitive stress during user interactions, especially in smart office environments.

EC4.3.1.name: Visual Continuity and Transparency
EC4.3.1.definition: Circulation zones maintain open sightlines and visual access to exits to reduce stress and disorientation.
EC4.3.1.justification: Open sightlines and visible exits directly reduce anxiety, confusion, and feelings of entrapment, making this the most important factor for intuitive and stress-free navigation.

EC4.3.2.name: Smart Emotional Navigation Aids
EC4.3.2.definition: Smart systems adapt navigation feedback (color, tone, brightness) to user-selected comfort preferences.
EC4.3.2.justification: Personalized navigation feedback enhances comfort and usability by adapting environmental communication to individual emotional preferences, but it functions mainly as a supportive smart feature.

EC4.4.1.name: Calm Visual Design
EC4.4.1.definition: Interfaces avoid high-contrast flashing colors, using balanced tones and consistent color palettes to reduce stress.
EC4.4.1.justification: Calm and visually stable interfaces reduce anxiety, sensory stress, and cognitive fatigue during repeated interaction with smart building systems.

EC4.4.2.name: Inclusive Communication Tools
EC4.4.2.definition: Systems provide optional speech-to-text, text-to-speech, or chat-based interaction for users with speech limitations.
EC4.4.2.justification: Speech-to-text, text-to-speech, and chat-based interaction tools directly support communication accessibility and independent use of services for users with speech or communication limitations.

EC4.5.1.name: Calm Acoustic Environment
EC4.5.1.definition: Sound levels ≤ 45 dB(A) and use of sound-absorbing materials reduce stress and improve communication clarity.
EC4.5.1.justification: Controlled acoustic conditions are fundamental for reducing stress, improving concentration, and supporting clear communication in office environments. Excessive noise is one of the strongest environmental stressors affecting mental wellbeing.

EC4.5.2.name: Positive Sensory Stimulation
EC4.5.2.definition: Art, light, and ambient sound are curated to encourage positive mood and reduce anxiety.
EC4.5.2.justification: Carefully curated sensory elements improve mood, emotional comfort, and overall user experience, but they function mainly as supportive enhancements to the environment.

EC5.1.1.name: Real-Time Accessibility Notifications
EC5.1.1.definition: Building users receive digital alerts (app, display) when accessible paths are blocked.
EC5.1.1.justification: Immediate notification of blocked or inaccessible routes is essential for maintaining safe and uninterrupted movement within dynamic office environments.

EC5.1.2.name: Dynamic Wayfinding Update
EC5.1.2.definition: Digital twin wayfinding updates automatically when temporary changes occur.
EC5.1.2.justification: Automatically updated wayfinding systems provide the strongest support for adaptive navigation when temporary spatial changes occur, making this the most influential criterion.

EC5.1.3.name: Inclusive Information Delivery
EC5.1.3.definition: Physical and digital notices use icons, audio, and text synchronously.
EC5.1.3.justification: Multiformat information delivery improves accessibility for diverse users, but it primarily supports communication effectiveness rather than direct spatial adaptation.

EC5.2.1.name: Dynamic Obstacle Monitoring
EC5.2.1.definition: Smart monitoring detects and alerts when circulation routes are obstructed, ensuring continuous accessibility.
EC5.2.1.justification: Continuous monitoring of circulation routes is critical for maintaining safe and uninterrupted accessibility in dynamic office environments where temporary obstructions frequently occur.

EC5.2.2.name: Assistive Technology Integration
EC5.2.2.definition: All digital and mechanical systems (e.g., doors, kiosks, lifts) are interoperable with assistive and personal devices.
EC5.2.2.justification: Interoperability with assistive devices significantly improves usability and independence, ensuring users can interact effectively with smart building systems and services.

EC5.3.1.name: Accessible Temporary Layouts
EC5.3.1.definition: Pop-up installations, furniture, or event setups maintain legible circulation patterns and accessible signage.
EC5.3.1.justification: Maintaining accessible circulation and understandable layouts during temporary changes is essential for preserving baseline accessibility and reducing confusion.

EC5.3.2.name: Smart Dynamic Wayfinding
EC5.3.2.definition: Real-time navigation updates through digital apps or screens adapt routes to temporary closures or hazards.
EC5.3.2.justification: Real-time adaptive navigation provides the strongest support for safe and efficient movement when routes change due to temporary closures, hazards, or operational adjustments.

EC5.3.3.name: Crowd Flow Visualization
EC5.3.3.definition: Smart displays or lighting signals indicate real-time density to guide users toward less congested routes.
EC5.3.3.justification: Real-time crowd-density guidance improves comfort, safety, and route selection, especially for users affected by stress, mobility limitations, or situational impairments.

EC5.4.1.name: Offline Function Continuity
EC5.4.1.definition: Core smart functions (access, lighting, security) remain operational in offline or low-connectivity conditions.
EC5.4.1.justification: Maintaining core building functions during connectivity failures is essential for continuous accessibility, safety, and independent building use.

EC5.4.2.name: Adaptive Font and Display Size
EC5.4.2.definition: Users can resize text, icons, and interface elements dynamically without losing layout consistency.
EC5.4.2.justification: Adjustable interface elements improve usability for diverse temporary or situational accessibility needs, but they mainly support interface personalization rather than operational continuity.

EC5.4.3.name: Emergency Digital Redundancy
EC5.4.3.definition: Backup power ensures continued operation of digital communication and alert systems during outages.
EC5.4.3.justification: Backup operation of communication and alert systems during emergencies is critical for life safety, emergency coordination, and uninterrupted access to essential building information.

EC5.5.1.name: Environmental Adaptability
EC5.5.1.definition: Lighting, sound, and thermal settings in social zones can be user-controlled or automatically adjusted to situational needs.
EC5.5.1.justification: User-adjustable environmental conditions directly influence comfort, stress reduction, usability, and inclusive participation in social and collaborative office spaces.

EC5.5.2.name: Dynamic Crowd Management
EC5.5.2.definition: Real-time occupancy and crowd flow are displayed visually to allow users to select low-density participation times.
EC5.5.2.justification: Real-time crowd information helps users avoid congestion, reduce stress, and select more comfortable participation conditions, especially for situational or temporary accessibility needs.
